In mathematics, '''Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem''' is one of several [[Ergodic theory#Ergodic theorems|ergodic theorems]]. It can be seen as a generalization of [[Ergodic theory#Ergodic theorems|Birkhoff's ergodic theorem]].<ref name="proof1">S. Lalley, Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem lecture notes, http://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/Graz/Kingman.pdf</ref>
Intuitively, the subadditive ergodic theorem is a kind of [[random variable]] version of [[Subadditivity#Properties|Fekete's lemma]] (hence the name ergodic).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://math.nyu.edu/degree/undergrad/Chen.pdf|title=Subadditive ergodic theorems|author=Chen|publisher=New York University}}</ref> As a result, it can be rephrased in the language of probability, e.g. using a sequence of random variables and [[expected value]]s.  The theorem is named after [[John Kingman]].

==Statement of theorem==
Let <math>T</math> be a [[Measure-preserving dynamical system|measure-preserving transformation]] on the [[probability space]] <math>(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)</math>, and let <math>\{g_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}</math> be a sequence of <math>L^1</math> functions such that <math>g_{n+m}(x)\le g_n(x)+g_m(T^nx)</math> (subadditivity relation). Then

: <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{g_n(x)}{n}=:g(x)\ge-\infty</math>

for <math>\mu</math>-a.e. ''x'', where ''g''(''x'') is ''T''-invariant. 

In particular, if ''T'' is [[ergodicity|ergodic]], then ''g''(''x'') is a constant.

=== Equivalent statement ===

Given a family of real random variables <math display="inline">X(m, n)</math>, with <math display="inline">0 \leq m < n \in \N</math>, such that they are subadditive in the sense that<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
      & X(m+1, n+1)=X(m, n) \circ T \\
      & X(0, n) \leq X(0, m)+X(m, n)
      \end{aligned}</math>Then there exists a random variable <math display="inline">Y</math> such that <math display="inline">Y \in [-\infty, +\infty)</math>, <math display="inline">Y</math> is invariant with respect to <math display="inline">T</math>, and <math display="inline">\lim_n \frac 1n X(0, n) = Y</math> a.s.. 

They are equivalent by setting

* <math display="inline">g_n = X(0, n)</math> with <math display="inline">n \geq 1</math>;
* <math display="inline">X(m, m+n) = g_n \circ T^m</math> with <math display="inline">m \geq 0</math>.
== Proof ==
Proof due to ([[J. Michael Steele]], 1989).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Steele |first=J. Michael |date=1989 |title=Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem |url=http://www-stat.wharton.upenn.edu/~steele/Publications/PDF/Steele_AIHPB_1989.pdf |journal=Annales de l'I.H.P. Probabilités et statistiques |language=en |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=93–98 |issn=1778-7017 |archive-date=2006-09-05 |access-date=2024-01-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060905180629/http://www-stat.wharton.upenn.edu/~steele/Publications/PDF/Steele_AIHPB_1989.pdf |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>

=== Subadditivity by partition ===
Fix some <math display="inline">n\geq 1</math>. By subadditivity, for any <math display="inline">l\in 1:n-1</math> <math display="block">
          g_n \leq g_{n-l} + g_l \circ T^{n-l}
          </math> 

We can picture this as starting with the set <math display="inline">0:n-1</math>, and then removing its length<math display="inline">l</math> tail.

Repeating this construction until the set <math display="inline">0:n-1</math> is all gone, we have a one-to-one correspondence between upper bounds of <math display="inline">g_n</math> and partitions of <math display="inline">1:n-1</math>.

Specifically, let <math display="inline">\{k_i : (k_i + l_i - 1)\}_i</math> be a partition of <math display="inline">0:n-1</math>, then we have <math display="block">
          g_n \leq \sum_i g_{l_i}\circ T^{k_i}
          </math>

=== Constructing ''g'' ===
Let <math display="inline">g := \liminf g_n/n</math>, then it is <math display="inline">T</math>-invariant.

By subadditivity, <math display="block">\frac{g_{n+1}}{n+1} \leq\frac{g_1 + g_n \circ T}{n+1}</math>  

Taking the <math display="inline">n\to \infty</math> limit, we have <math display="block">g \leq g\circ T</math> We can visualize <math display="inline">T</math> as hill-climbing on the graph of <math display="inline">g</math>. If <math display="inline">T</math> actually causes a nontrivial amount of hill-climbing, then we would get a spatial contraction, and so <math display="inline">T</math> does not preserve measure. Therefore <math display="inline">g = g\circ T</math> a.e.

Let <math display="inline">c\in \R</math>, then <math display="block">\{g \geq c\} \subset \{g\circ T \geq c\} = T^{-1}(\{g \geq c\})</math> and since both sides have the same measure, by squeezing, they are equal a.e..

That is, <math display="inline">g(x) \geq c \iff g(Tx) \geq c</math>, a.e..

Now apply this for all rational <math display="inline">c</math>.

=== Reducing to the case of ''g<sub>n</sub> ≤ 0'' ===


By subadditivity, using the partition of <math display="inline">0:n-1</math> into singletons. <math display="block">
          \begin{aligned}
          g_1 &\leq g_1 \\
          g_2 &\leq g_1 + g_1 \circ T \\
          g_3 &\leq g_1 + g_1 \circ T + g_1 \circ T^2 \\
          & \cdots  
          \end{aligned}
          </math> Now, construct the sequence <math display="block">
          \begin{aligned}
          f_1 &= g_1 - g_1 \\
          f_2 &= g_2 - (g_1 + g_1 \circ T) \\
          f_3 &= g_3 - (g_1 + g_1 \circ T + g_1 \circ T^2) \\
          & \cdots  
          \end{aligned}
          </math> which satisfies <math display="inline">f_n \leq 0</math> for all <math display="inline">n</math>.

By the special case, <math display="inline">f_n/n</math> converges a.e. to a <math display="inline">T</math>-invariant function.

By Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem, the running average <math display="block">\frac 1n (g_1 + g_1 \circ T + g_1 \circ T^2 + \cdots ) </math>converges a.e. to a <math display="inline">T</math>-invariant function. Therefore, their sum does as well.

=== Bounding the truncation ===
Fix arbitrary <math display="inline">\epsilon, M > 0</math>, and construct the truncated function, still <math display="inline">T</math>-invariant: <math display="block">g' := \max(g, -M)</math> With these, it suffices to prove an a.e. upper bound<math display="block">\limsup g_n/n \leq g' + \epsilon</math>since it would allow us to take the limit <math display="inline">\epsilon = 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots</math>, then the limit <math display="inline">M = 1, 2, 3, \dots</math>, giving us a.e.

<math display="block">
      \limsup g_n/n \leq \liminf g_n/n =: g
      </math>And by squeezing, we have <math display="inline">g_n/n</math> converging a.e. to <math display="inline">g</math>.
Define two families of sets, one shrinking to the [[empty set]], and one growing to the full set. For each "length" <math>L = 1, 2, 3, \dots</math>, define<math display="block">B_L := \{x : g_l/l > g' + \epsilon, \forall l \in 1, 2, \dots, L\}</math> <math display="block">A_L := B_L^c = \{x : g_l/l \leq g' + \epsilon, \exists l \in 1, 2, \dots, L\}</math>Since <math display="inline">g' \geq \liminf g_n/n</math>, the <math display="inline">B</math> family shrinks to the empty set.


Fix <math display="inline">x \in X</math>. Fix <math display="inline">L \in \N</math>. Fix <math display="inline">n > L</math>. The ordering of these qualifiers is vitally important, because we will be removing the qualifiers one by one in the reverse order.

To prove the a.e. upper bound, we must use the subadditivity, which means we must construct a partition of the set <math display="inline">0:n-1</math>. We do this inductively:<blockquote>Take the smallest <math display="inline">k</math> not already in a partition.</blockquote><blockquote>If <math display="inline">T^k x \in A_N</math>, then <math display="inline">g_l(T^k x)/l \leq g'(x) + \epsilon</math> for some <math display="inline">l\in 1, 2, \dots L</math>. Take one such <math display="inline">l</math> – the choice does not matter.</blockquote><blockquote>If <math display="inline">k+l-1 \leq n-1</math>, then we cut out <math display="inline">\{k, \dots, k+l-1\}</math>. Call these partitions "type 1". Else, we cut out <math display="inline">\{k\}</math>. Call these partitions "type 2".</blockquote><blockquote>Else, we cut out <math display="inline">\{k\}</math>. Call these partitions "type 3".</blockquote>

Now convert this partition into an inequality: <math display="block">
          g_n(x) \leq \sum_i g_{l_i}(T^{k_i}x)
          </math> where <math display="inline">k_i</math> are the heads of the partitions, and <math display="inline">l_i</math> are the lengths.

Since all <math display="inline">g_n \leq 0</math>, we can remove the other kinds of partitions: <math display="block">
          g_n(x) \leq \sum_{i: \text{type 1}} g_{l_i}(T^{k_i}x)
          </math> By construction, each <math display="inline">g_{l_i}(T^{k_i}x) \leq l_i(g'(x) + \epsilon)</math>, thus <math display="block">
          \frac 1n g_n(x) \leq g'(x) \frac 1n \sum_{i: \text{type 1}} l_i + \epsilon
          </math> Now it would be tempting to continue with <math display="inline">g'(x) \frac 1n \sum_{i: \text{type 1}} l_i \leq g'(x)</math>, but unfortunately <math display="inline">g' \leq 0</math>, so the direction is the exact opposite. We must ''lower'' bound the sum <math display="inline">\sum_{i: \text{type 1}} l_i</math>.

The number of type 3 elements is equal to<math display="block">
              \sum_{k\in 0:n-1} 1_{B_L}(T^k x)
              </math>If a number <math display="inline">k</math> is of type 2, then it must be inside the last <math display="inline">L-1</math> elements of <math display="inline">0:n-1</math>. Thus the number of type 2 elements is at most <math display="inline">L-1</math>. 
Together, we have the ''lower'' bound:<math display="block">
          \frac 1n  \sum_{i: \text{type 1}} l_i \geq 1 - \frac{L-1}{n} - \frac 1n \sum_{k\in 0:n-1} 1_{B_L}(T^k x)
          </math> 

=== Peeling off the first qualifier ===
Remove the <math display="inline">n>L</math> qualifier by taking the <math display="inline">n\to \infty</math> limit.

By Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem, there exists an a.e. pointwise limit<math display="block">
\lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{k\in 0:n-1} 1_{B_L}(T^k x) \to \bar 1_{B_L}(x)
          </math>  satisfying<br />
<math display="block">
          \int \bar 1_{B_L}  = \mu(B_L); \quad \bar 1_{B_L}(x) \in [0, 1]
          </math> At the limit, we find that for a.e. <math display="inline">x\in X, L \in \N</math>, <math display="block">
          \limsup_n \frac{g_n(x)}{n} \leq g'(x) (1- \bar 1_{B_L}(x) )  + \epsilon
          </math>

=== Peeling off the second qualifier ===
Remove the <math display="inline">L \in \N</math> qualifier by taking the <math display="inline">L\to \infty</math> limit.

Since we have <math display="block">
          \int \bar 1_{B_L}  = \mu(B_L) \to 0
          </math>and <math>\bar 1_{B_L} \geq \bar 1_{B_{L+1}} \geq \cdots</math> as <math>1_{B_{L}} \geq 1_{B_{L+1}} \geq \cdots</math>, we can apply the same argument used for proving [[Markov's inequality]], to obtain<br /><math display="block">
          \limsup_n \frac{g_n(x)}{n} \leq g'(x)  + \epsilon
          </math>
for a.e. <math display="inline">x\in X</math>.


In detail, the argument is as follows: since <math>\bar 1_{B_L} \geq \bar 1_{B_{L+1}} \geq \cdots \geq 0</math>, and <math> \int \bar 1_{B_L} \to 0</math>, we know that for any small <math>\delta, \delta' > 0</math>, all large enough <math>L</math> satisfies <math>\bar 1_{B_L}(x) < \delta</math> everywhere except on a set of size <math>\geq \delta'</math>. Thus,<math display="block">
          \limsup_n \frac{g_n(x)}{n} \leq g'(x)(1-\delta)  + \epsilon
          </math>with probability <math>\geq 1-\delta'</math>. Now take both <math>\delta, \delta' \to 0</math>.

==Applications==
Taking <math>g_n(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}f(T^jx)</math> recovers Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem.

Taking all <math>g_n</math> constant functions, we recover the Fekete's subadditive lemma.

Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem can be used to prove statements about [[Lyapunov exponent]]s. It also has applications to [[Percolation theory|percolations]] and [[longest increasing subsequence]].<ref>Pitman, Lecture 12: Subadditive ergodic theory, http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~pitman/s205s03/lecture12.pdf</ref>

=== Longest increasing subsequence ===
To study the longest increasing subsequence of a random permutation <math>\pi</math>, we generate it in an equivalent way. A [[random permutation]] on <math>1:n</math> is equivalently generated by uniformly sampling <math>n</math> points in a square, then find the longest increasing subsequence of that.

Now, define the [[Poisson point process]] with density 1 on <math>[0, \infty)^2</math>, and define the random variables <math>M^*_k</math> to be the length of the longest increasing subsequence in the square <math>[0, k)^2</math>. Define the measure-preserving transform <math>T</math> by shifting the plane by <math>(-1, -1)</math>, then chopping off the parts that have fallen out of <math>[0, \infty)^2</math>.

The process is subadditive, that is, <math> M_{k+m}^* \geq M_{k}^* + M_{m}^* \circ T^k</math>. To see this, notice that the right side constructs an increasing subsequence first in the square <math>[0, k)^2</math>, then in the square <math>[k, k+m)^2</math>, and finally concatenate them together. This produces an increasing subsequence in <math>[0, k+m)^2</math>, but not necessarily the longest one. 

Also, <math>T</math> is ergodic, so by Kingman's theorem, <math>M_k^* /k</math> converges to a constant almost surely. Since at the limit, there are <math>n = k^2</math> points in the square, we have <math>L_n^* / \sqrt n</math> converging to a constant almost surely.
